AI video editing: a guide to the five agents
A practical guide to AI video editing: what the five agents do and how to brief them.

AI video editing works best when it is organized like a post-production team: each specialist has one craft, and all of them share one brief. Kaviyan is built that way. Five AI agents (Cut, Hue, Nova, Echo and Flow) work inside the editing software you already use, on your own timeline. This guide explains what each agent does, how to brief them, and where a human editor should still make the call.
What AI video editing does, and what it leaves to you

An AI video editor is strongest at the first pass and the repeated pass: assembling selects, matching shots, cleaning audio, resizing for another format. It does not decide what the story is. In Kaviyan every cut, grade and effect the agents make stays fully editable, so the editor keeps the final word on each one.
The five agents and their crafts

Three ways to brief the agents
The same five agents take a brief in three forms, and you can switch between them at any point in a project.
A template: start from a finished structure and replace the footage.
A sentence: describe the video in plain words, such as “a 30 second product teaser with fast cuts and bold captions”.
A script: paste the script, and the agents build the edit around it line by line.
A good brief names the audience, the length, the format and one reference. Leave out adjectives that a camera could not record.
A first project, step by step
Import. Drop in your footage, or let Nova generate the shots you are missing.
Edit. Ask Cut for a rough cut, then move, swap and trim until the story holds.
Enhance. Run Hue for the grade and Echo for the sound.
Ship. Let Flow add titles and motion, then export for each channel.
Run one agent or all five on the same timeline. Each agent picks up where the last one left off, so nothing is exported or rebuilt between steps.

Agents are fast at drafts and consistent at repetition. Taste remains a human job. Watch the opening five seconds yourself, check every generated shot against the brand, and listen to the mix on a phone speaker before it ships. Teams that keep those three checks get the speed without losing their voice.
You do not need to know how to edit video to start. The free plan includes unlimited drafts and watermark-free exports up to 1080p, which is enough to finish a first project and judge the result.

Maison Vire: 120 localized videos in one sprint
One hero film, nine markets, a single sprint: how the video localization was run.

Maison Vire is a fashion house that sells in nine markets, and every seasonal campaign has to arrive in all of them on the same day. This season the team delivered 120 localized edits from one hero film in a single two-week sprint. A year earlier, the same video localization took most of a quarter.
Why video localization used to take a quarter

Each market needs its own titles, prices, currency and legal lines. Each channel needs its own aspect ratio. In past seasons Maison Vire’s editors duplicated the master project for every market, replaced the text by hand and exported each version three times. Feedback arrived by email, often about the wrong file.

Sara Lindqvist, Creative Director at Maison Vire, counted the cost after the spring campaign: eleven weeks from locked edit to the last regional delivery. By then the collection had been in stores for a month.

For the autumn campaign the team changed the order of work. The hero film and its three cut-downs were finished and approved first, in one project, inside the editing software the team already used. Every market-specific element then went into a single sheet: one row per market, one column per title, price and legal line.
Kaviyan’s agents read that sheet as their brief.
Cut reframed each edit for horizontal, square and vertical formats and re-timed the cut-downs.
Flow replaced titles, captions, price cards and legal lines for each market, in the brand’s own motion style.
Hue held the approved grade across every version, so no market drifted warmer or cooler.
Echo rebalanced the mix under each new voice-over.
Where a vertical crop lost the product, Nova generated a new insert shot from a prompt, and the editors approved it like any other shot.
How the 120 localized edits add up

Every market received the hero film and three cut-downs in three aspect ratios. That is 108 edits. The four largest markets also received an extended brand film in all three ratios, which adds twelve more. No version was built by hand, and every one stayed fully editable on the timeline.
“Nine markets, three aspect ratios, one sprint,” says Lindqvist. “Localization stopped being a quarter-long project and became a checklist.”

Regional teams reviewed their own versions through review links, with each comment pinned to the frame it was about. A corrected price in one market changed one row in the sheet, and Flow updated that market’s edits. Nothing else had to be exported again.
The last market signed off on day nine of the sprint. The remaining days went to exports: MP4 for social channels, ProRes for broadcast and in-store screens.
What Maison Vire would tell another brand team
Lock the master edit before localizing anything.
Keep every market-specific line in one sheet, owned by one person.
Let regional teams review their own cuts on the timeline, not in email.
Treat the first sprint as setup. The next season reuses the same blocks.
Maison Vire now plans localization as a checklist at the end of each campaign, not as a project of its own. The winter campaign is already scheduled the same way.

How Northfold ships 4× more social cuts
A six-person team rebuilt its social media video editing around five AI agents.
Teal monster character in a straw hat

Northfold is an entertainment studio with a six-person content team and a release calendar that never slows down. A year ago the team shipped about twelve social cuts a week. Today it ships fifty. Nobody was hired, and nobody works later. What changed is how Northfold handles social media video editing: the repetitive first pass belongs to Kaviyan’s AI agents, and the editors keep the decisions.
Where the week used to go

Daniel Okafor, Head of Content at Northfold, describes the old routine plainly. Every Monday went to rough cuts. Editors pulled selects from the weekend’s footage, built an assembly for each show, then rebuilt the same intro, lower thirds and end card for every format. A note on one title meant opening five projects instead of one.
The team was skilled, but most of its hours went to work that looked identical from week to week. First cuts reached review on Wednesday. By Friday the calendar was already behind.
A first assembly before the editors arrive

Northfold connected Kaviyan to the editing software it already used, so nothing had to be exported or rebuilt. Weekend footage goes into a project on Sunday night. Cut, the editing agent, builds a rough cut for each episode, trims dead air and tightens the pacing. When the editors sit down on Monday, a first assembly is waiting on the timeline.
“We used to spend Mondays on rough cuts,” says Okafor. “Now Cut has a first assembly waiting, and a full social edit ships in an afternoon.”
The assembly is a starting point, not a verdict. Every cut stays editable, and the editors still move scenes, swap takes and change the ending. They begin with a draft instead of an empty timeline.
Lower thirds that live as reusable blocks

The second change was quieter. Northfold moved its recurring pieces (intros, lower thirds, captions and end cards) into shared blocks. Flow, the motion agent, places and animates them in every cut, sized for each aspect ratio. When a show changes its typeface or a sponsor changes its logo, the block is updated once and every cut that uses it follows.
Hue matches the grade across cameras, and Echo cleans the dialogue and balances the music bed. A cut that leaves the timeline already looks and sounds like Northfold.
How social media video editing runs at Northfold now
The weekly routine is short enough to fit in a list.
Sunday night: weekend footage goes into the project, and Cut prepares a first assembly for each episode.
Monday morning: the editors review the assemblies and shape the story.
Monday afternoon: Hue grades, Echo mixes, and Flow adds titles, captions and lower thirds from the shared blocks.
Before the day ends: the edit is exported in every format the channels need, up to 4K at 60fps.
A full social edit now ships in an afternoon. The rest of the week goes to work the team used to postpone: longer features, new formats and experiments.
Weekly output rose from 12 social cuts to 50, a little more than four times as many.
First assemblies are ready before the working week starts.
A brand change is made in one block instead of in every project.
The team is still six people.

Okafor’s advice to other content teams is to start with the most repeated task, not the most impressive one. For Northfold that was the rough cut and the lower third. Once those two ran on their own, the rest of the pipeline followed.
Teams that want the same setup can start on the free plan, or ask Kaviyan Studio to build the first blocks with them.

Product update: reusable video editing workflows
Chain Cut, Hue, Echo and Flow into one saved video editing workflow and reuse it.

Most teams repeat the same sequence on every video: rough cut, grade, sound, titles, export. As of this release, that sequence can be saved. Workflows chain Kaviyan’s agents into one reusable video editing workflow that runs on any new project from a single brief.
What a video editing workflow is in Kaviyan

A workflow is an ordered chain of agents with your settings attached. A typical one reads like this: Cut builds a 30 second rough cut, Hue applies the brand look, Echo mixes the music under the dialogue, Flow adds captions and the end card, and the result is exported in three aspect ratios. Each step hands its timeline to the next, so nothing is exported or rebuilt in between.
Workflows run inside the editing software you already use, through Editor Sync. The output is a normal timeline, and every cut, grade and effect on it stays editable.
What is new in this release
Saved workflows. Build a chain once, name it and reuse it on any project.
Review steps. Pause the chain after any agent, check the result and continue.
Team sharing. Publish a workflow to your workspace so every editor starts from the same chain.
Batch runs. Point one workflow at a folder of footage and get a draft for each clip.
Export sets. Attach formats to a workflow: MP4, MOV, ProRes, GIF, PNG sequences or stills, up to 4K at 60fps.
How to build your first workflow
Open a finished project that you are happy with.
Choose Save as workflow. Kaviyan lists the agents you used, in order, with their settings.
Remove what was specific to that project, and add a review step wherever you want to check the work.
Name the workflow and share it with your team.
Run it on the next project: drop in the footage and write one sentence about the video.
The first run takes about as long as briefing each agent yourself. The saving starts with the second project.
An example workflow for a weekly series

A team that publishes one episode a week might save a chain called Weekly Social. Cut assembles a 45 second edit from the long recording and keeps the strongest opening line. A review step pauses the chain so an editor can approve the story. Hue then applies the series look, Echo levels the voices and brings the theme music in under the last line, and Flow adds the captions, the lower third and the end card. The export set delivers horizontal, square and vertical versions in one pass.
Workflows are included in the Studio and Scale plans and are live in every workspace on those plans. Free and Creator workspaces can still run the agents one after another by hand.

When we looked at how teams used the agents, one pattern kept returning. Editors ran the same four or five steps in the same order, with the same settings, and typed the same brief every time. Workflows turn that habit into something a team can save, share and improve.
Lena Hartmann, our founder, has one rule for every release: “Every tool we ship has to save an editor an hour, or it doesn’t ship.” Workflows apply that rule to the brief itself.
Next we are working on scheduled runs, so a workflow can start as soon as new footage arrives. Requests are welcome at viyako.designs@gmail.com.
